passage:
Sunday, 2 a.m.

Friday I promised myself never again. I wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it to the mirror. Last night I drank again anyway. Woke up hating myself. I said things in my head I'd never say to a friend: weak, pathetic, useless.

And then I noticed something: every time I feel like that, the next thing I want is another drink, just to switch off the voice. The hating is part of the loop.

Chaitanya texted this morning, "Call me anytime. No lecture." I hadn't told Chaitanya anything, but somehow it landed.

So tonight I'm writing it as facts: Friday, alone, after the fight with my sister. That's a trigger. Tomorrow I'll call Chaitanya and ask about the campus counsellor.

Pradeep

qa.q: What did Pradeep write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Pradeep wrote a promise of never again on a sticky note and stuck it to the mirror.

qa.q: What does Pradeep notice about the hating feeling, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The self-hate makes Pradeep want another drink to switch off the voice, so the shame is part of the loop instead of a cure.

qa.q: What steps is Pradeep planning, and how do they treat the relapse?
qa.a: Pradeep treats it as data, naming the trigger of Friday alone after the fight with the sister, then plans to call Chaitanya and ask about the campus counsellor.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Pradeep's struggle?
qa.a: Chaitanya seems to sense something is wrong and offers a call with no lecture, so support without judgement is what Chaitanya wants to give. 🤍

grounding: After each binge Pradeep promises never again and relapses with self-hatred, then sees shame fuels the cycle, treats relapse as data and seeks support.

passage:
In Bhadrak, after the shop closed at nine, Binita scrolled. Short videos, one after another, until the call to prayer from the mosque told her it was nearly dawn. Every morning she promised herself: never again. Every night she broke it. By the third week she was calling herself useless out loud, and scrolling more to escape that voice.

On Sunday her cousin Swati found her asleep at the counter. Binita cried and told her everything.

Swati didn't scold. "Okay. So when does it start? What happens right before?"

They worked it out together: it started when she was tired and alone after closing. So Swati began calling at nine. The phone charged in the kitchen at night. And on Monday Swati went with her to the college counsellor.

On Wednesday Binita slipped again. This time she wrote down what had set it off.

qa.q: Who found Binita asleep at the counter?
How did Binita feel about herself during the third week?
qa.a: Binita felt ashamed and full of self-hate, calling herself useless and scrolling more to escape that voice.

qa.q: What did Swati and Binita try, and why does it help?
qa.a: They found the trigger, being tired and alone after closing, then planned calls, charging the phone in the kitchen, and seeing a counsellor, so relapse becomes information rather than failure.

qa.q: How might Swati see Binita's slip on Wednesday?
qa.a: Swati is likely to see it as part of recovery, not a failure, especially since Binita wrote down what set it off.

grounding: The story shows a young woman caught in a shame-and-binge cycle who gets support, plans for triggers and treats a relapse as information.

passage:
Every Sunday morning in her Manchester flat, Nour woke with a pounding head, deleted the photos from the night before and told herself, never again. By Thursday the promise felt thin. By Saturday she was out again, drinking until she couldn't remember the walk home, and on Sunday the voice was harsher: you're pathetic, you have no control.

Liam found her on the kitchen floor one Sunday, crying into a mug of tea. He didn't lecture. "Hating yourself hasn't worked so far. Can we try something else?"

They sat with a notebook. Every binge came after a week of skipped lectures and no sleep, when she felt behind and alone. On Monday Nour went to the university wellbeing service and joined a Wednesday recovery group. Liam agreed to text her on Saturday evenings. The first slip came two weeks later. This time she wrote down what happened before it.

qa.q: Where did Liam find Nour one Sunday?
qa.a: Liam found her on the kitchen floor, crying into a mug of tea.

qa.q: How did Nour feel on Sundays after a binge?
qa.a: Nour felt deep shame and self-hatred, hearing a harsh voice call her pathetic and out of control.

qa.q: Why was Liam's approach better than a lecture?
qa.a: Liam pointed out that self-hatred had not worked and helped her spot triggers and get support, which breaks the cycle instead of feeding it.

qa.q: How might Liam feel when he sees Nour on the kitchen floor?
qa.a: Liam likely feels worried and sad for her, but calm enough to offer a practical next step instead of blame.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose shame after each binge fuels relapse, who begins to treat slips as information and gets support.
